name: 1. Discovery and planning
description: Problem, audience, goals, scope, budget, timeline.

cards.subject: A problem statement
says: names who has the problem, what they are trying to do and what gets in the way
is short enough for everyone on the team to repeat from memory
cards.use: need the whole team to share one view of why the project exists
not: lists the features that will be built

cards.subject: A pain point
says: is a specific frustration a person meets while doing a task
is found by watching or asking people rather than by guessing
cards.use: hear users complain about the same step again and again
not: is the same thing as a requested feature

cards.subject: A current workaround
says: shows how people cope today without the new product
is evidence that the problem is real enough for people to spend effort on it
reveals the true cost of the problem in time or errors
cards.use: need to check that a problem is real before proposing a project
not: is a sign that the problem can safely be ignored

cards.subject: The problem space
says: describes the needs and constraints before any answer is chosen
is explored through research with the people who have the problem
cards.use: want to understand a need without committing to an answer
not: lists the possible technologies for the build

cards.subject: The solution space
says: holds the possible ways of meeting a need
is narrowed by constraints such as budget, time and skills
cards.use: have a clear problem and need to compare options
not: is explored before the problem is understood

cards.subject: Jobs to be done
says: frames demand as the progress a person is trying to make in a circumstance
explains why people switch to a product by the situation they were in
cards.use: find that demographics do not explain why people choose a product
not: segments customers mainly by age and job title

cards.subject: Root cause analysis
says: looks for the underlying reason a problem happens rather than its visible symptom
aims to stop the problem recurring instead of patching one instance
cards.use: keep fixing the same problem and it keeps coming back
not: stops at the first cause that anyone suggests

cards.subject: The five whys
says: asks why repeatedly, usually about five times, to move from symptom to cause
needs no tools beyond a conversation
cards.use: want a quick way to dig below a symptom in a short meeting
not: guarantees that exactly one root cause exists

cards.subject: Solution bias
says: is jumping to a favoured answer before the problem is understood
often appears as a request phrased as a specific screen or tool
cards.use: hear a stakeholder ask for a particular feature without describing the need behind it
not: happens only when a team has too little technical skill

cards.subject: The opportunity cost of doing nothing
says: is the loss that keeps accumulating if no project is started
gives a baseline to compare every option against
cards.use: need to justify a project that looks optional
not: is always zero when no money is spent

cards.subject: Impact mapping
says: links a goal to the actors, the changes in their behaviour and the deliverables that might cause them
helps remove deliverables that do not trace back to a goal
cards.use: suspect that half the proposed features do not serve the stated goal
not: ranks backlog items by their estimated effort alone

cards.subject: A how-might-we question
says: turns a problem into an open question that invites several answers
avoids naming a solution inside the question
cards.use: want a workshop to generate options instead of defending one idea
not: is a closed question answered with yes or no

cards.subject: The user
says: is the person who touches the product in daily work
feels friction in the workflow before anyone else does
cards.use: need to learn what the daily task is really like
not: is always the person who pays for the product

cards.subject: The buyer
says: is the person or group that pays for the product
cares about cost, risk and evidence of return
cards.use: must convince the person holding the budget
not: necessarily uses the product every day

cards.subject: The administrator
says: controls access, settings and accounts for other people
is easy to forget in discovery even though the rollout depends on them
cards.use: find that setup and permissions are someone else's job
not: is the same person as the sponsor

cards.subject: A stakeholder
says: is anyone who is affected by the project or can affect it
is wider than the people who attend the project meetings
cards.use: need to list everyone with an interest in the outcome
not: is limited to the people who fund the project

cards.subject: A project sponsor
says: provides funding and senior authority for the project
removes blockers that the team cannot clear alone
cards.use: need a decision that is above the project manager's authority
not: writes the code and tests it

cards.subject: A persona
says: is a composite profile built from research on real users
gives the team a shared picture of a type of user
cards.use: want the team to design for a type of user rather than for themselves
not: is a real named customer who signed a contract

cards.subject: A power and interest grid
says: plots stakeholders by their influence and their interest
suggests whom to manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed or monitor
cards.use: have more stakeholders than time and must decide where to spend effort
not: measures how satisfied each stakeholder is with the product

cards.subject: A RACI chart
says: assigns responsible, accountable, consulted and informed roles
allows only one accountable person for each task
cards.use: find that two people each assume the other owns a decision
not: ranks stakeholders by their budget

cards.subject: A hidden stakeholder
says: is a group affected by the outcome that never appears in the meetings
is often a team such as support or operations that will run the result
cards.use: realise that the team that will run the system was never asked
not: is a user who deliberately avoids the product

cards.subject: A gatekeeper
says: can block a launch without owning the project
is typically a function such as security, legal or procurement
cards.use: find that a late review can stop a finished project
not: supplies the funding for the project

cards.subject: A champion
says: is an internal advocate who helps others adopt the change
gives the team credibility with the people they want to reach
cards.use: need a trusted voice inside the user group to help the rollout
not: is paid by the vendor to promote the product

cards.subject: An anti-persona
says: describes who the product is deliberately not built for
helps the team refuse requests that pull the product away from its audience
cards.use: keep receiving feature requests from people outside the target audience
not: is a user who dislikes the product

cards.subject: A user interview
says: is a one-to-one conversation that explores a person's experience and reasons
is best used to learn why people behave as they do
cards.use: need to understand the reasons behind behaviour
not: produces statistically reliable counts of how many people agree

cards.subject: A survey
says: collects answers from many people with the same fixed questions
gives numbers but little depth about reasons
cards.use: need to measure how common an attitude is across a large group
not: reveals the unexpected reasons behind a single person's behaviour

cards.subject: Contextual inquiry
says: observes people doing the task in their own setting
reveals steps and workarounds that people forget to mention
cards.use: suspect that what people say differs from what they do at their desks
not: is carried out in a meeting room with a question list

cards.subject: Support ticket analysis
says: mines existing requests for recurring problems and the words customers use
gives evidence without a new round of fieldwork
cards.use: want evidence of real problems quickly and cheaply
not: shows what people who never contact support think

cards.subject: Competitor analysis
says: compares how other products and substitutes meet the same need
includes the spreadsheet or manual process as a competitor
cards.use: need to know what people use today and what they would switch from
not: copies a rival's feature list into the scope

cards.subject: An analytics review
says: looks at recorded behaviour such as drop-off points and frequency
shows what people do but not why
cards.use: have a live product and want to find where users give up
not: explains the motivation behind each click

cards.subject: A prototype test
says: puts a rough version in front of users to see if they can complete a task
is cheaper than building the real feature first
cards.use: want evidence about a design before committing build time
not: proves the system will scale to production load

cards.subject: A diary study
says: asks participants to record their experiences over days or weeks
captures events that are too infrequent or private to observe directly
cards.use: need to understand a habit that unfolds over weeks
not: is finished in a single one-hour session

cards.subject: A focus group
says: gathers several people to discuss a topic together
can be dominated by the loudest voice in the room
cards.use: want to hear how people react to ideas in conversation with each other
not: is the best way to observe individual task behaviour

cards.subject: A leading question
says: suggests the answer the asker hopes to hear
can be avoided by asking about past behaviour instead of opinions
cards.use: notice that interview answers keep agreeing with your idea
not: is a question with no right answer

cards.subject: Confirmation bias
says: makes people notice the evidence that supports what they already believe
is reduced by actively looking for evidence that disproves the idea
cards.use: catch yourself counting only the interviews that agree with the plan
not: affects only inexperienced researchers

cards.subject: Sampling bias
says: occurs when the people studied do not represent the real audience
happens when you only talk to the users who are easy to reach
cards.use: realise all your interviewees were colleagues or friendly customers
not: is removed by increasing the number of similar participants

cards.subject: Survivorship bias
says: comes from studying only those who stayed and ignoring those who left
hides why people abandoned the product
cards.use: have feedback only from current customers and want to understand churn
not: means the sample was chosen at random

cards.subject: The say-do gap
says: is the difference between what people claim they will do and what they do
is why observed behaviour is trusted above stated intent
cards.use: hear that 80 percent say they would pay but nobody has yet
not: only occurs when participants are lying on purpose

cards.subject: The HiPPO effect
says: lets the highest paid person's opinion override evidence
is countered by agreeing the decision criteria before the discussion
cards.use: find that the senior person's view settles every debate
not: describes a decision made by averaging everyone's votes

cards.subject: An outcome
says: is a change in behaviour or results that people experience
is what the project is ultimately judged on
cards.use: need to describe the result you want rather than the thing you build
not: is something the team ships

cards.subject: An output
says: is something the team produces, such as a dashboard
can be delivered without anyone's situation improving
cards.use: report what was built rather than what changed
not: is the measured change in user behaviour

cards.subject: A baseline
says: is the measured starting value before any change
is what makes an improvement provable
cards.use: cannot tell whether the project improved anything
not: is the target value the team hopes to reach

cards.subject: A target
says: is the value the measure should reach by a stated time
is set against a baseline
cards.use: need to say how much improvement counts as success
not: is the starting value recorded before the project

cards.subject: A KPI
says: is a key indicator tracked over time against an objective
should be collected in a way the team has agreed in advance
cards.use: need a small number of measures to report progress regularly
not: is any number that can be pulled from a database

cards.subject: OKRs
says: pair an inspiring objective with a few measurable key results
separate what you want to achieve from how it is measured
cards.use: want a goal framework that links ambition to measurable results
not: list the tasks that each person will complete

cards.subject: A leading indicator
says: moves early and predicts a later result
can be influenced by the team soon enough to act on it
cards.use: cannot wait months for the real result to see whether you are on track
not: reports what has already happened

cards.subject: A lagging indicator
says: reports a result after it has happened
confirms success but arrives too late to steer
cards.use: need to confirm whether the goal was reached
not: predicts results before they occur

cards.subject: A vanity metric
says: looks impressive but does not guide any decision
tends to rise whatever the team does, such as total sign-ups
cards.use: notice that a number only ever goes up and nobody acts on it
not: is an actionable measure tied to a decision

cards.subject: A guardrail metric
says: is a measure that must not get worse while the target improves
catches harm caused by chasing a single goal
cards.use: worry that speeding up a process may reduce its quality
not: is the main success target of the project

cards.subject: A north star metric
says: is the one measure that best captures the value delivered to users
aligns several teams on a single direction
cards.use: want every team to pull toward one shared measure of value
not: is always a revenue figure

cards.subject: Goodhart's law
says: says a measure stops being a good measure once it becomes a target
explains why people begin to game a number they are rewarded for
cards.use: see staff closing tickets quickly without solving them
not: says that every target improves performance

cards.subject: Scope
says: is the list of what is in and what is out of the project
gives the team an agreed boundary to check requests against
cards.use: need to agree what the project will and will not deliver
not: is the same as the budget of the project

cards.subject: An MVP
says: is the smallest complete version that lets real users do the main job
is built to teach the team something as well as to deliver value
cards.use: want to release the smallest thing that lets users complete the core journey
not: is a half-finished version of the full product

cards.subject: A non-goal
says: is something the project deliberately will not do
protects the team when someone asks for one more feature
cards.use: need a ready answer when asked to add an extra capability
not: is a goal the team failed to reach

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is uncontrolled growth of the scope after it was agreed
usually arrives as many small requests that each look reasonable
cards.use: find that the deliverables keep growing while the deadline stays fixed
not: is a deliberate, approved addition to the scope

cards.subject: A change request
says: is a formal proposal to alter agreed scope, cost or timeline
forces the trade-off to be seen before the change is accepted
cards.use: get a late request that would move the date
not: is a defect report on delivered work

cards.subject: A work breakdown structure
says: divides the project into smaller deliverables until each can be estimated
is organised by deliverable rather than by calendar date
cards.use: cannot estimate a large piece of work as one number
not: is a calendar of tasks against dates

cards.subject: A user story map
says: arranges user activities across the top and the details beneath
helps choose a thin slice that covers the whole journey
cards.use: need to see the whole journey while deciding what to build first
not: lists backlog items in a single ranked column

cards.subject: A vertical slice
says: delivers a thin piece that runs through every layer from interface to data
shows real working behaviour early
cards.use: want working software that touches every layer, even if narrow
not: completes one entire layer before touching the next

cards.subject: A walking skeleton
says: is a minimal implementation of the architecture that connects the main components end to end
lets the team test deployment and integration very early
cards.use: want to prove the main pieces connect before building features
not: delivers the finished user experience for one feature

cards.subject: Gold plating
says: is adding polish or features nobody asked for
adds cost and risk without clear value
cards.use: see a developer improve something the user never requested
not: is the agreed process of delivering requested work

cards.subject: MoSCoW
says: sorts requirements into must, should, could and will not have
makes the must-haves the line below which the project fails
cards.use: need a quick way to agree what is essential for the first release
not: scores items using reach, impact, confidence and effort

cards.subject: RICE scoring
says: scores items on reach, impact, confidence and effort
divides expected benefit by the effort
cards.use: must compare many ideas with a repeatable numerical score
not: sorts items into four named buckets without scores

cards.subject: The Kano model
says: separates basic expectations, performance features and delighters
shows that some features only avoid dissatisfaction rather than add delight
cards.use: wonder whether a feature is a basic expectation or a delighter
not: scores items by cost of delay divided by job size

cards.subject: Weighted shortest job first
says: divides the cost of delay by the job size
favours short high-value items to reduce the total delay cost
cards.use: have items of different sizes and want the order that cuts the total delay cost
not: groups requirements as must, should, could and will not

cards.subject: Cost of delay
says: is the value lost for each period a feature is not available
makes timing an input to prioritisation rather than an afterthought
cards.use: need to compare a small urgent item against a large valuable one
not: is the money spent on development

cards.subject: A value and effort matrix
says: plots items by the value they give and the effort they need
highlights quick wins as high value for low effort
cards.use: want a simple visual way of picking quick wins
not: gives a single number for each idea

cards.subject: Stack ranking
says: puts every item into a single ordered list
forces a choice because no two items can tie
cards.use: find that everything is called high priority
not: allows several items to share the top priority

cards.subject: An estimate range
says: states a lower and upper bound with its assumptions
communicates uncertainty honestly
cards.use: are asked for a number when much is still unknown
not: promises a single committed date

cards.subject: A three-point estimate
says: uses best, likely and worst case values for each piece of work
shows how wide the uncertainty is
cards.use: need to estimate a task whose duration varies a lot
not: uses only the most likely value

cards.subject: PERT
says: weights the likely case more heavily when combining three estimates
uses the formula of optimistic plus four times likely plus pessimistic, divided by six
cards.use: want a weighted average from three estimates
not: takes the plain average of the best and worst cases

cards.subject: Planning poker
says: has team members reveal estimates at the same time
discussion follows when the cards differ widely
cards.use: want to avoid one person anchoring everyone's estimate
not: lets the most senior person announce the figure first

cards.subject: T-shirt sizing
says: uses sizes such as small, medium and large for a rough relative estimate
is suited to early stages when precise numbers are not possible
cards.use: need a quick rough order of magnitude for many items
not: gives hour-level precision

cards.subject: Analogous estimation
says: bases an estimate on similar past work
is quick but only as good as the similarity
cards.use: have little detail but have completed something similar before
not: builds the total by adding up every small task

cards.subject: Bottom-up estimation
says: adds together estimates of the smallest tasks
needs a work breakdown first
cards.use: have detailed scope and need an accurate figure
not: compares the project to one finished earlier

cards.subject: The cone of uncertainty
says: shows the estimate range narrowing as the project progresses
explains why early estimates carry a wide range
cards.use: have to explain why the estimate was far off at the start
not: says that estimates are always accurate after approval

cards.subject: Reference class forecasting
says: uses the outcomes of many similar past projects to set expectations
corrects the optimism of a plan built only from the inside view
cards.use: suspect that your plan is more optimistic than similar projects have been
not: relies on the team's own detailed task list

cards.subject: The planning fallacy
says: is the tendency to underestimate time even when past projects overran
is partly countered by looking at similar past projects
cards.use: see that every previous project ran late yet the new plan assumes it will not
not: is a mistake only beginners make

cards.subject: A contingency buffer
says: is time or money reserved for the risks you can name
is held and released by someone accountable
cards.use: need room for known risks without padding every task
not: is hidden inside each task estimate

cards.subject: The critical path
says: is the longest chain of dependent tasks
sets the shortest possible project duration
cards.use: need to know which delays will move the end date
not: is the list of the most important features

cards.subject: Parkinson's law
says: says work expands to fill the time available
explains why padding every task rarely produces early finishes
cards.use: see that a task given a generous deadline is finished exactly on it
not: says that tasks are always completed early

cards.subject: A risk
says: is an uncertain event that could affect the project, for good or ill
has a probability and an impact
cards.use: need to describe something that might happen
not: is a problem that has already happened

cards.subject: An issue
says: is a problem that has already happened
needs action now rather than monitoring
cards.use: find that a supplier has already missed its delivery
not: is something that might happen in future

cards.subject: An assumption
says: is something taken as true without proof
should be written down so it can be tested
cards.use: are planning on the basis of something you have not checked
not: is a verified fact backed by evidence

cards.subject: A constraint
says: is a fixed limit such as a deadline, a budget or a rule
is not up for negotiation within the project
cards.use: have a launch date fixed by an external event
not: is an uncertain event that might happen

cards.subject: A dependency
says: is a task or deliverable that relies on something outside the team
should be listed early so slow ones can start first
cards.use: need an approval or credentials that someone else controls
not: is a risk with a low probability

cards.subject: A risk register
says: lists risks with their probability, impact, owner and response
is reviewed regularly rather than written once
cards.use: need a shared record of what could go wrong and who is watching it
not: is a list of defects found in testing

cards.subject: A probability and impact matrix
says: rates each risk on likelihood and consequence
helps decide which risks need action first
cards.use: have a long risk list and need to decide where to look first
not: records which person owns each risk

cards.subject: Risk mitigation
says: reduces the probability or the impact of a risk
works by changing the plan, the design or the process so the exposure is smaller
cards.use: can take a step now that makes a risk less likely or less damaging
not: decides to live with the risk

cards.subject: Risk acceptance
says: is the conscious decision to live with a risk and its consequences
is sensible when the cost of a response exceeds the risk
cards.use: face a small risk where the response costs more than the loss
not: means the risk was never noticed

cards.subject: Risk transference
says: shifts the impact of a risk to a third party, for example through insurance or a contract
does not remove the risk, only who bears the cost
cards.use: want a supplier or insurer to carry the financial consequences
not: makes the risk less likely to occur

cards.subject: A premortem
says: asks the team to imagine the project has failed and explain why
brings out concerns that people hold back in optimistic planning
cards.use: want the team to name its worries before the project starts
not: reviews the causes of a failure after it happened

cards.subject: The riskiest assumption test
says: tests the belief that would sink the project if it were false
is done first, with the cheapest experiment possible
cards.use: have a long assumption list and must decide what to test first
not: tests the easiest assumption first

cards.subject: Residual risk
says: is the risk that remains after the response has been applied
needs to be accepted explicitly by someone
cards.use: have applied controls and still see some exposure
not: is the risk before any action is taken

cards.subject: A feasibility study
says: assesses whether a project can be done before full commitment
covers technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule questions
cards.use: need to decide whether an idea is worth pursuing before funding it
not: plans the day-by-day tasks of the build

cards.subject: Technical feasibility
says: asks whether the team can build it with the skills and technology available
is checked by experiments on the hardest parts
cards.use: doubt that the team's tools can do what the idea needs
not: asks whether the benefits outweigh the costs

cards.subject: Economic feasibility
says: asks whether the benefits justify the costs
compares the cost of build and operation with the value gained
cards.use: need to confirm the project makes financial sense
not: asks whether the technology exists

cards.subject: Operational feasibility
says: asks whether the organisation can run and adopt the result
includes training, support and changes to working processes
cards.use: worry that the team will build it but nobody can run it
not: checks that the code compiles

cards.subject: Legal feasibility
says: asks whether the project complies with laws, contracts and regulations
can prevent a project from proceeding at all
cards.use: suspect that the idea touches personal data or a regulated activity
not: checks whether the schedule is achievable

cards.subject: Schedule feasibility
says: asks whether the work can be completed by the required date
tests whether the deadline is consistent with the estimates and dependencies
cards.use: have a fixed date and must check that it is achievable
not: checks that the licence terms are acceptable

cards.subject: A proof of concept
says: shows that an idea can work in principle
is usually thrown away once the question is answered
cards.use: need to prove a risky technical idea works before committing to it
not: is the first release delivered to customers

cards.subject: A technical spike
says: is a short time-boxed investigation to answer a specific technical question
produces knowledge, not production code
cards.use: need an answer on an unfamiliar technology within a day or two
not: delivers a shippable feature

cards.subject: A go or no-go decision
says: is the point where sponsors decide whether to proceed with the project
is made on the evidence gathered in discovery
cards.use: reach the end of discovery and must decide whether to fund the build
not: is made after the product has launched

cards.subject: A cost-benefit analysis
says: compares total expected costs with total expected benefits
expresses both in the same units, usually money
cards.use: need to compare the value of an option with what it costs
not: lists every feature the project will deliver

cards.subject: A payback period
says: is the time taken for the benefits to recover the initial cost
ignores what happens after the break-even point
cards.use: want to know how soon an investment pays for itself
not: discounts future cash flows to today's value

cards.subject: Net present value
says: discounts future benefits and costs to today's value
is positive when discounted benefits exceed discounted costs
cards.use: must compare options with benefits that arrive in different years
not: measures the months until break-even

cards.subject: A build-or-buy decision
says: chooses between developing a solution and acquiring one
should consider the lifetime cost, not only the starting price
cards.use: must decide whether to write software or purchase a product
not: is made once and never revisited

cards.subject: Total cost of ownership
says: includes purchase, integration, operation, support and eventual replacement
is usually larger than the licence or build cost alone
cards.use: find that the cheapest price on the page is not the cheapest option
not: is the price quoted on the vendor's website

cards.subject: Vendor lock-in
says: makes switching supplier costly because of proprietary formats or integrations
is weighed when choosing a platform
cards.use: worry that leaving a supplier later would be very expensive
not: guarantees the best price over time

cards.subject: A core capability
says: is what differentiates the organisation, so it is usually worth building
is not something to hand to a supplier whose roadmap you cannot influence
cards.use: consider building something that competitors cannot copy by buying it
not: is a commodity function such as payroll

cards.subject: A commodity capability
says: is a function that many organisations need in the same way
is usually cheaper to buy than to build
cards.use: consider a feature that gives no advantage over competitors
not: is the source of the organisation's unique advantage

cards.subject: Integration cost
says: is the effort of connecting a bought product to existing systems and data
is often underestimated at the buying stage
cards.use: find that the bought product still needs weeks of connecting work
not: is the licence fee for the product

cards.subject: Data portability
says: is the ability to export your data in a usable form
is checked before signing, as part of an exit plan
cards.use: want to be sure you can leave a supplier with your data
not: means the supplier hosts the data in your region

cards.subject: A vendor trial
says: tests a bought product against real tasks before commitment
produces evidence rather than relying on a sales demonstration
cards.use: are shown an impressive demo and want proof it fits your work
not: replaces the contract negotiation

cards.subject: The sunk cost fallacy
says: lets money already spent push a team to continue a failing path
is avoided by deciding on future costs and benefits only
cards.use: hear "we have already spent so much" as the reason to carry on
not: means that earlier spending should always decide the next step

cards.subject: The maintenance burden
says: is the ongoing cost of fixing, patching and supporting what you build
falls on your own team when you choose to build
cards.use: are tempted by a build option and forget who looks after it later
not: falls entirely on the vendor when you build

cards.subject: A project charter
says: is a short document that authorises the project and names its sponsor
records the purpose, goals, scope, high-level risks and key stakeholders
cards.use: need a one-page agreement on why the project exists and who backs it
not: lists the detailed technical design

cards.subject: A statement of work
says: defines the work, deliverables and terms agreed with a supplier
is the document a contract refers to for what is delivered
cards.use: engage an external supplier and need the deliverables written down
not: authorises the internal project without a contract

cards.subject: A business case
says: justifies the investment with costs, benefits, options and risks
supports the go or no-go decision
cards.use: must persuade the funders that the project is worth the money
not: describes how the software will be tested

cards.subject: A product brief
says: summarises the problem, audience, goals and scope on one or two pages
is short enough that everyone actually reads it
cards.use: want a short common reference at the start of a project
not: lists the full technical requirements

cards.subject: A project plan
says: sets out tasks, owners, dependencies and dates
is revised as the work and the knowledge change
cards.use: need to show who does what and by when
not: is fixed for the life of the project

cards.subject: A product roadmap
says: shows the planned direction in themes over time
is a statement of intent rather than a promise
cards.use: want to communicate direction without committing to exact dates
not: is a detailed list of tasks per developer

cards.subject: A communication plan
says: states who needs what information, how often and through which channel
reduces surprises for stakeholders
cards.use: find that some stakeholders hear news only when it is too late
not: is a list of the project risks

cards.subject: A Gantt chart
says: shows tasks as bars against a calendar
makes dependencies and overlaps visible
cards.use: need to see how tasks overlap over time
not: ranks tasks by value

cards.subject: A milestone
says: marks a significant point or checkpoint in the project
has no duration of its own
cards.use: want a checkpoint to see if the project is on track
not: is a task that takes several weeks

cards.subject: A decision log
says: records what was decided, by whom, when and why
stops the same debate from being repeated months later
cards.use: hear a decision questioned and nobody remembers the reason
not: is a list of open issues awaiting action

cards.subject: A discovery report
says: summarises what research found, what is still assumed and what is recommended
gives the funders what they need to decide on the build
cards.use: finish discovery and must hand the findings to the decision makers
not: is the final user manual of the product

cards.subject: A kickoff meeting
says: brings the team and stakeholders together at the start of delivery
confirms the goals, scope, roles and ways of working
cards.use: want everyone to start from the same understanding
not: is held after the product has launched

cards.subject: A kickoff agenda
says: covers the problem, goals, scope, roles, risks and next steps
ends with named owners and dates for the first actions
cards.use: need a kickoff that leaves everyone knowing what happens next
not: consists only of a presentation by the sponsor

cards.subject: A working agreement
says: records how the team will communicate, decide and handle disagreement
is created by the team rather than imposed
cards.use: want the team to agree its own rules of working
not: is a contract with an external supplier

cards.subject: A definition of done
says: is the shared checklist a piece of work must meet to count as complete
stops different people using different standards
cards.use: find that people argue about whether something is finished
not: lists what is ready to be started

cards.subject: A definition of ready
says: is the shared checklist an item meets before the team accepts it
avoids starting work that is unclear or blocked
cards.use: find that the team starts items that are missing key information
not: states when work is considered finished

cards.subject: An escalation path
says: says who to go to when a problem cannot be resolved at the team level
is agreed before it is needed
cards.use: hit a blocker that no one in the team can remove
not: is a list of the risks the team has accepted

cards.subject: A single source of truth
says: is one agreed place where the current plan and decisions live
avoids conflicting copies of documents
cards.use: find that people are working from different versions of the plan
not: is a backup of every document

cards.subject: Discovery exit criteria
says: state what must be known before the project moves from discovery to delivery
prevent discovery from continuing without end
cards.use: want to know when discovery is finished
not: are the acceptance tests for the product

cards.subject: A communication cadence
says: sets a regular rhythm for updates and reviews
keeps stakeholders informed without asking each time
cards.use: want stakeholders to know when the next update will arrive
not: is a single announcement at launch

cards.subject: The ggmoney status table
says: marks each capability as working, needs credentials or not built
lets a reader see at once what exists today
cards.use: want stakeholders to see exactly what is built and what is not
not: hides unfinished capabilities until they are ready

cards.subject: Corporation Tax in ggmoney
says: is marked Not built and planned for a later phase
is stated plainly rather than hinted at
cards.use: need an example of labelling a missing feature honestly
not: is described as working but needing credentials

cards.subject: The gglearn Known gaps section
says: lists the limits of the project, including thin high levels in the legacy question bank
gives a ready answer when someone asks what is missing
cards.use: want the limits written down early to stop stakeholders assuming features exist
not: is a list of defects fixed in the last release

cards.subject: SQLite in gglearn
says: is used for local development
is to be replaced by Postgres before multi-user production use
cards.use: want to delay a bigger commitment until it is needed
not: is the chosen production database for many users

cards.subject: Mark planned as planned
says: means anything planned is labelled planned and never as done
protects trust when stakeholders read the status
cards.use: are tempted to describe a future feature as if it exists
not: allows rounding a half-built feature up to done

cards.subject: The two-sentence problem statement
says: fits in two sentences so everyone can repeat it
is the company's test of whether the team shares one view
cards.use: need a quick test of whether the team understands the problem
not: is written as a full page of background

cards.subject: Facts and assumptions kept apart
says: records what was learned as facts and keeps assumptions on a separate list
lets the assumptions be tested later
cards.use: find that a project plan mixes known facts with guesses
not: merges every note into one undifferentiated list

cards.subject: The onboarding example goal
says: cuts new-starter onboarding from five days to two
shows an outcome with a baseline and a target
cards.use: need an example of a goal with a measure, a baseline and a target
not: says to build an onboarding dashboard

cards.subject: Cut scope, not testing
says: is the rule of reducing work instead of quality when time is short
keeps testing and review in the plan under deadline pressure
cards.use: are told the date cannot move and quality is tempting to trim
not: says to skip review so the date is met

cards.subject: Start the slow dependencies first
says: begins waits such as approvals, credentials and suppliers early
puts the longest external delays at the front of the plan
cards.use: depend on an external approval that takes weeks
not: leaves approvals until just before launch

cards.subject: A review at launch and again weeks later
says: checks the goals at launch and again after a few weeks
shows whether early enthusiasm turned into real use
cards.use: want to know whether launch excitement became lasting use
not: is a single review on launch day

qa.q: What should discovery start with?
qa.right: A problem, not a solution
qa.why: Discovery explores the problem and the people who have it before any answer is picked.

qa.q: Which statement best describes an MVP?
qa.right: The smallest complete version that lets real users do the main job
wrong: A half-finished version of the full product
A prototype that is discarded after one demo
The version with every planned feature but no polish
qa.why: An MVP is small but complete for the core journey.

qa.q: What is an assumption in a project plan?
qa.right: Something taken as true without proof, to be tested
wrong: A fixed limit such as a deadline
A problem that has already occurred
qa.why: Assumptions need to be written down so they can be tested.

qa.q: Who are stakeholders?
qa.right: Anyone affected by the project or able to affect it
wrong: Only the people who fund it
qa.why: The group is wider than the people who attend meetings.

qa.q: Which is an outcome rather than an output?
qa.right: People spot problems a day earlier
qa.why: Outcomes are changes in behaviour or results; outputs are things produced.

qa.q: Why give an early estimate as a range?
qa.right: Because uncertainty is high and the range shows it honestly
wrong: Because ranges are easier to calculate
qa.why: Early information is limited, so a single number implies false precision.

qa.q: Which pair describes the difference between a risk and an issue?
qa.right: A risk might happen; an issue has already happened
wrong: A risk is technical; an issue is financial
A risk is internal; an issue is external
A risk is permanent; an issue is temporary
qa.why: Risks are uncertain; issues are current problems.

qa.q: What does a baseline make possible?
qa.right: Proving that a measure improved
qa.why: Without a starting value, you cannot tell whether anything changed.

qa.q: What is the best use of a user interview?
qa.right: Learning why people behave as they do
wrong: Measuring how many people hold an opinion
qa.why: Interviews give depth about reasons, not reliable counts.

qa.q: Which technique has team members reveal estimates at the same moment?
qa.right: Planning poker
qa.why: Simultaneous reveal prevents anchoring on the first number spoken.

qa.q: What does MoSCoW sort requirements into?
qa.right: Must, should, could and will not have
qa.why: MoSCoW is a four-bucket prioritisation method.

qa.q: What is a non-goal?
qa.right: Something the project deliberately will not do
wrong: A goal owned by another team
qa.why: Non-goals protect the team from one-more-feature requests.

qa.q: A project charter mainly does what?
qa.right: Authorises the project and records its purpose, goals, scope and sponsor
wrong: Lists every technical task and its estimate
Defines acceptance tests for each feature
Describes how the system is deployed
qa.why: A charter is a short agreement on why the project exists and who backs it.

qa.q: Which formula does PERT use for the expected duration?
qa.right: (optimistic + 4 x likely + pessimistic) / 6
qa.why: PERT weights the likely case four times.

qa.q: A team is told that 80 percent of surveyed customers would pay for a feature, but nobody has paid yet. Which concept applies?
qa.right: The say-do gap
qa.why: Stated intent often differs from actual behaviour.

qa.q: Which describes a leading indicator?
qa.right: A measure that moves early and predicts a later result
wrong: A measure reported after results are final
qa.why: Leading indicators give the team time to act.

qa.q: What is the main purpose of a technical spike?
qa.right: To answer a specific technical question within a short time box
qa.why: A spike produces knowledge rather than production code.

qa.q: Which best describes a proof of concept?
qa.right: A demonstration that an idea can work in principle
wrong: A complete product with fewer features
qa.why: A proof of concept answers feasibility and is often discarded.

qa.q: What does a RACI chart allow for each task?
qa.right: Only one accountable person
qa.why: Multiple people can be responsible, but accountability sits with one.

qa.q: What does a probability and impact matrix help you decide?
qa.right: Which risks need attention first
wrong: How much budget the project needs
Which tasks are on the critical path
qa.why: It rates risks on likelihood and consequence to rank them.

qa.q: What does total cost of ownership include?
qa.right: Purchase, integration, operation, support and replacement
wrong: Only the cost of developer time
qa.why: Lifetime costs often exceed the headline price.

qa.q: Which is a commodity capability for most organisations?
qa.right: Payroll processing
wrong: The algorithm behind a unique product
The customer experience that sets the brand apart
A proprietary pricing engine that wins customers
qa.why: Commodity functions are needed in the same way by many and are usually bought.

qa.q: Which of these is a correct use of a change request?
qa.right: Making the trade-off of a late scope change visible before accepting it
wrong: Recording a bug found in testing
qa.why: Change requests force a conscious trade-off.

qa.q: In the five whys technique, what are you trying to move from?
qa.right: A symptom toward an underlying cause
qa.why: Repeated why questions dig beneath the visible problem.

qa.q: Which risk response describes buying insurance against a loss?
qa.right: Transference
qa.why: Transference moves the cost of impact to a third party without removing the risk.

qa.q: What does reference class forecasting correct?
qa.right: The optimism of a plan built only from the inside view
qa.why: It anchors on outcomes of similar past projects.

qa.q: What is the key difference between a walking skeleton and an MVP?
qa.right: A walking skeleton proves the architecture connects end to end; an MVP delivers value to real users
wrong: A walking skeleton is bigger than an MVP
A walking skeleton includes every feature
qa.why: The skeleton tests integration and deployment early with minimal behaviour.

qa.q: Which of these is a guardrail metric for a project to speed up support responses?
qa.right: Customer satisfaction with the answers
qa.why: A guardrail must not worsen while the target improves.

qa.q: Which discount-based measure compares options with benefits in different years?
qa.right: Net present value
qa.why: NPV discounts future cash flows to today's value.

qa.q: Which method would you choose to rank many ideas with a repeatable numeric score?
qa.right: RICE scoring
qa.why: RICE scores reach, impact, confidence and effort.

qa.q: A bonus is paid for closing support tickets quickly and staff begin closing them without solving them. Which law describes this?
qa.right: Goodhart's law
qa.why: A measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure.

qa.q: Which residual risk statement is correct?
qa.right: It is the risk that remains after the response has been applied
wrong: It is the risk before any action is taken
It is a risk that has been transferred completely
It is a risk with zero probability
qa.why: Residual risk is what is left after controls.

qa.q: A stakeholder says "we need a dashboard". What should you do first?
qa.right: Ask what decision or problem the dashboard is meant to help with
wrong: Estimate the dashboard and start building
Ask which charting library they prefer
Add it to the backlog as a must-have
qa.why: A request phrased as a solution hides the need; discovery starts with the problem.

qa.q: A team is asked for a delivery date when only a few sentences of scope exist. What is the most useful reply?
qa.right: Give a range with the assumptions, and say when it will narrow
wrong: Give the most optimistic single date
Refuse to estimate until all the detail is known
Double the developers' first guess and call it firm
qa.why: Ranges with assumptions are honest about uncertainty.

qa.q: All of your interviewees are colleagues who like the idea. What is the problem?
qa.right: Sampling bias, because they do not represent the real audience
wrong: Scope creep, because the sample keeps growing
The cone of uncertainty, because the number is small
qa.why: The sample is unrepresentative, so it cannot confirm demand.

qa.q: A project needs credentials from a third party that normally take three weeks. What should the plan do?
qa.right: Request them at the start so the wait does not block later work
wrong: Leave the request until the code is ready
Assume they will arrive on time
Remove the dependency from the plan
qa.why: Slow external dependencies should be started first.

qa.q: A sales leader insists the product needs a feature because a prospect asked for it. You have no other evidence. What is the best response?
qa.right: Treat it as an assumption, test how common the need is and decide on evidence
wrong: Add it to the scope because the request is senior
Reject it because it was not in the original plan
Ask the prospect to design the feature
qa.why: One request is not evidence of demand; test the assumption.

qa.q: Halfway through, a stakeholder adds a small request that would move the date. How should you handle it?
qa.right: Raise a change request that shows the cost and schedule trade-off before deciding
wrong: Absorb it quietly to keep the stakeholder happy
Refuse all changes after the kickoff
Move the date without telling anyone
qa.why: A visible trade-off lets the sponsor choose.

qa.q: A team's plan has every task padded and the project still finishes on the last day. What best explains this?
qa.right: Parkinson's law, work expands to fill the time available
qa.why: Padding each task hides slack that is then consumed.

qa.q: A vendor product costs less to buy than to build but needs a year of integration work. What should the team compare?
qa.right: The total cost of ownership of each option
wrong: Only the licence price against the build cost
Only the number of features offered
qa.why: Integration and operation costs belong in the comparison.

qa.q: The team keeps arguing about whether a ticket is finished. What would help?
qa.right: A shared definition of done
qa.why: A common checklist stops people using different standards.

qa.q: You hear "we have already spent six months, we cannot stop now". What is the best response?
qa.right: Decide using the future costs and benefits only, because the past spending cannot be recovered
wrong: Continue because stopping wastes the money
Double the budget to finish quickly
Ask the vendor for a refund
qa.why: This is the sunk cost fallacy.

qa.q: Customer feedback comes only from people who are still subscribed. What does that miss?
qa.right: The reasons why people left
qa.why: Studying only survivors hides the cause of churn.

qa.q: A discovery report shows the biggest risk is that users will not trust automated advice. Which action addresses the riskiest assumption first?
qa.right: Run a cheap prototype test of whether users act on the advice
wrong: Build the full system and see
qa.why: Test the belief that would sink the project, with the cheapest experiment.

qa.q: Sponsors want one number to track a service improvement project. The team fears a single target will be gamed. What is a sound approach?
qa.right: Pair the target with a guardrail metric
wrong: Pick a measure that cannot be counted
qa.why: A guardrail catches harm caused by chasing a single number.

qa.q: A premortem is run and the team names a risk nobody voiced before. What should happen next?
qa.right: Add it to the risk register with an owner and a response
wrong: Ignore it because the project has not failed
Record it only in the minutes
qa.why: The point is to bring concerns out and assign action.

qa.q: A sponsor reads a plan and sees that Corporation Tax is not shown. Another report marks it as Not built, planned for a later phase. Which habit does the second report show?
qa.right: Honest scoping: planned items are labelled planned, not done
qa.why: Writing limits down early stops stakeholders assuming features exist.

qa.q: In the gglearn project, which statement fits the README's Known gaps approach?
qa.right: Limits are recorded in writing so stakeholders do not assume missing features exist
wrong: Gaps are left out so that the product looks complete
Gaps are discussed only after launch
Gaps are fixed before the README is written
qa.why: Writing limits down early gives a ready answer when someone asks.

qa.q: The gglearn project uses SQLite for local development and says to move to Postgres before multi-user production use. What planning idea does this show?
qa.right: Deferring a costlier commitment until it is needed
wrong: Choosing the final database before discovery
qa.why: Deferring costly choices can be sensible if the trigger for change is written down.

qa.q: Deadlines are fixed and the team is behind. Following the company's approach, what do you cut?
qa.right: Scope, not testing
qa.why: Reduce the work rather than the quality when time is short.

qa.q: What is the best test of a goal such as "reduce onboarding from five days to two"?
qa.right: It has a measure, a baseline and a target
wrong: It lists the features to be built
It has no number so it cannot fail
It is owned by a vendor
qa.why: A useful goal is an outcome with a baseline and a target.

qa.q: A team has a charter, a plan and a risk register but finds nobody agrees who decides trade-offs. Which artefact would fix it?
qa.right: A RACI chart with one accountable person per decision
qa.why: Accountability must be assigned to one person per task.

qa.q: Two stakeholders each believe the other will approve the security review. Which concept explains the gap?
qa.right: No single accountable owner was assigned
qa.why: RACI assigns exactly one accountable person.
